body:
Docker-in-sandbox is a high-risk surface from a behavioral perspective — not just because of the isolation implications, but because Docker API calls are a common exfiltration and lateral movement vector in agentic attacks.
An agent that gains Docker access can pull external images, spawn containers with different permission profiles, or exfiltrate data through volume mounts in ways that look individually legitimate but constitute an attack sequence in aggregate. Each action passes a single-action check but the sequence is the attack.
I'm building Zetra (zetra-openshell), a behavioral graph analysis layer on top of OpenShell's OCSF event stream (PR #489). One thing that would significantly help: routing Docker daemon API calls through the same OCSF event stream as other process and network activity. If Docker API calls surface as typed ProcessActivityEvent or NetworkActivityEvent entries, behavioral tools can detect anomalous Docker usage patterns — image pulls from unexpected registries, containers spawned outside normal workflow, volume mounts that match data staging patterns.
Without that, Docker becomes a blind spot in the behavioral graph. An agent could use it as an exfiltration channel that looks like normal container activity at the infrastructure level but is clearly anomalous at the behavioral sequence level.
Of the four approaches listed, option 4 (remote Docker / build delegation) is the most compatible with behavioral monitoring — proxying Docker API calls through a controlled layer gives you a natural interception point for OCSF event emission. Worth considering as an evaluation criterion alongside the security tradeoffs.
